Regarding legal, policy and institutional frameworks, the Independent Expert recommends that the Government: (a) Amend the Basic Law of Governance (Royal Decree No. A/90 (1992)) to explicitly prohibit age-based discrimination in all spheres of life; (b) Adopt a comprehensive, rights-based national strategy for older persons, including monitoring and accountability mechanisms, designed with the participation of older persons; (c) Create a national board for older persons, similar to the Authority for the Care of Persons with Disabilities, which would promote the implementation of the above-mentioned strategy, among others; (d) Bring the Human Rights Commission into full compliance with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (the Paris Principles), with a view to achieving accreditation with A status; (e) Ratify the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families, in line with the commitment expressed by the Government and the recommendation made in the context of the universal periodic review in 2024, and ensure the full alignment of national legislation and practices with its provisions; (f) Consider ratifying all core human rights treaties and optional protocols thereto, as well as the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees; (g) Ensure the systematic collection of data disaggregated by age, gender and other intersectional factors, as the foundation for targeted policy measures that respond to the needs of older persons.

records.text: 78. Saudi Arabia has embarked on an ambitious agenda of social development, guided by the Saudi Vision 2030 programme. The Independent Expert witnessed some of the advancements related to the human rights of older persons, and positively notes the efforts and results in relation to healthcare, education and the accessibility of infrastructure and government services, many of which could serve internationally as best practices. 79. The Independent Expert highlights the strong impact that the increasing rate of labour ‐ force participation is having among younger women in Saudi Arabia, which will contribute to the improvement of life in old age for future generations. At the same time, many older women who dedicated their lives to unpaid and unrecognized care work continue to rely heavily on family support to maintain their autonomy and well-being. Their contributions need to be recognized and addressed through inclusive, gender-sensitive policies that ensure that all women are able to age with dignity, security and independence. 80. Looking ahead, it is important to prepare for the evolving role of the family in the care of older persons, particularly as a result of ongoing urbanization, increasing work mobility and the growing participation of women in the labour market. Such efforts will require the development of community-based support systems, especially in rural and disadvantaged areas, offering accessible care services, information and transportation to ensure that older persons can continue to live with dignity and independence. 81. The human rights commitments of Saudi Arabia, as well as the Sustainable Development Goals, mean that meaningful social progress and advancements cannot be achieved with the exclusion of large parts of the population. Non-citizens comprise the largest part of the workforce in Saudi Arabia, and a third of its population of older persons. It is therefore urgent to redirect efforts for progress on the human rights of older persons to include those who are not Saudi citizens. As a result, two upcoming historical events during which Saudi Arabia will be in the international spotlight – Expo 2030 Riyadh and the 2034 FIFA World Cup – would be aligned with the country’s human rights obligations. Both events will largely depend on non-Saudi workers. The protection of their rights, both during their working life and after retirement, would be significantly enhanced with the ratification of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. This action could potentially make Saudi Arabia an example for the Gulf region, where most countries heavily rely on a foreign workforce. 82. Another group of older persons who are excluded from benefiting from the country’s efforts towards modernization are those who are arbitrarily arrested, imprisoned, often in inhumane conditions, and sentenced for opposing the Government or dissenting with its policies. The lack of data, transparency and monitoring of the legal processes affecting them and their conditions of detention remain a reason for great concern.

records.text: 73. In Saudi Arabia, the family plays a central role in the provision of support to older persons. The right to family life is central to the dignity, emotional well-being and autonomy of older persons, and includes the rights to maintain relationships with spouses, children and extended family, and to reside with or near loved ones, especially in times of increased care and support needs. The family can also be a crucial source of social protection and cultural identity. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (article 16), the family is recognized as the fundamental group unit of society, entitled to protection by society and the State. The Arab Charter on Human Rights affirms the right of individuals not to be arbitrarily expelled from their country of residence (art. 26) and the duty of the State and society to ensure the protection of the family (art. 33). The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women affirms equal rights for women in all matters relating to family life and residence (arts. 9, 15 and 16). The importance of the family is also emphasized in the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing, with regard to the strengthening of intergenerational ties at the family and community level (para. 43). 74. Despite the above, older non-citizen residents of Saudi Arabia, many of whom have lived and worked in the country for decades or were even born in the country, face structural and legal barriers that prevent the full enjoyment of the right to family life. These barriers include the absence of a comprehensive framework for family reunification, the lack of a pathway to long-term residency or regularization, and restrictive policies on visa and sponsorship after retirement. These limitations may result in the separation of families, undermining the right to family life and protections against arbitrary expulsion, under article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and article 26 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights. They also contradict the principles of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, in which States committed to facilitating family reunification, especially for migrants in vulnerable situations. 75. During the visit, the Independent Expert received information about older persons who have lived in Saudi Arabia for several decades but are unable to bring their families into the country owing to income thresholds. Others are forced to leave the country, even when they have lived their entire lives in Saudi Arabia, once they retire and lose their sponsorship. The Independent Expert was informed of cases of domestic workers who no longer had family ties with their countries of nationality, meaning that forcing them to leave Saudi Arabia would cut their only social connections and make them move to a place where they lacked any social network at a stage in life where social support was as crucial as ever. These situations disproportionately affect low-income workers and those who formerly worked in the informal sector, and may constitute discrimination on the basis of age and socioeconomic status. 76. Older women face additional barriers. Older non-citizen women may be denied the right to remain in the country after retirement unless their husbands or sons are able to sponsor them. Lacking independent legal status, they face the risk of deportation even after having contributed to the economy and society of Saudi Arabia, often as domestic workers providing care to older persons. 77. Respect for the right to family life, including for older non-citizens, is an essential component of building inclusive and age-friendly societies. In line with the commitments made under the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, facilitating access to procedures for family reunification would contribute not only to individual well-being, but also to the broader goals of social cohesion, intergenerational solidarity and sustainable development.

records.section: I. Education and economic inclusion of older persons
records.text: 69. The Independent Expert visited several initiatives offering opportunities to older persons to continue education, including vocational training, literacy and digital literacy. Several of these initiatives reach older persons in the remotest areas of the country and are highly valuable, especially for older persons who did not enjoy a formal education at a younger age. These efforts support the right to education for all and reflect the commitments under the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing, 2002 (paras. 12 (d) and 21 (c)) with regard to the provision of opportunities for lifelong learning to enhance the quality of life of older persons. Ensuring educational access in older age contributes not only to individual development and autonomy, but also to social participation. 70. Given the rapid digitalization of many aspects of life in Saudi Arabia, including government services, the digital literacy of older persons is of crucial importance to facilitate their autonomy and access to various human rights, such as the right of access to information, the right to a legal identity and the right to participate in the cultural life of the community. 71. Saudi Arabia does not have a mandatory retirement age, positively allowing older persons who wish to continue employment to do so while they are able and willing to work, in line with the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing (para. 23). Under the pension system of the General Organization for Social Insurance, pensions are provided to those retiring at the age of 60 and above and who have contributed for a minimum of five years. The retirement age has been increased to 65 for both women and men joining the General Organization for Social Insurance as new members. The Government informed the Independent Expert that it is planning incentives to keep older, experienced employees in the labour market and expand its efforts in upskilling and lifelong learning. This flexible approach is aligned with the right to work and to freely choose or accept employment, and supports target 8.5 of the Sustainable Development Goals, on achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all. However, policies must also ensure that older persons, including women and informal workers, who are unable to continue working have access to adequate pension benefits, in accordance with article 11 (1) (e) of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and article 28 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 72. The Independent Expert received information on numerous Government-supported initiatives for the economic participation of older persons in rural areas, such as in beekeeping and olive oil cooperatives. Under another positive initiative, the National Centre for Vegetation Cover Development and Combating Desertification, in Al-Jumum national park, which has regularly conducted outreach activities to include local older persons in its development, plans to provide employment to older persons and to allow older beekeepers to seasonally establish hives in the area. It has also conducted research to recover the knowledge among older persons on traditional crops that are resistant to droughts, making them suitable for climate change. These initiatives reflect how policies on ageing can be combined with climate resilience strategies, and highlight the important role that older persons play in the transmission of traditional knowledge, also including with regard to the environment. In accordance with the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing and the United Nations Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030), the inclusion of older persons in environmental and rural development projects not only advances their rights to work and to participation, but also contributes to goals on sustainability.

records.text: 65. Many interlocutors shared their impression with the Independent Expert that religion and cultural traditions in Saudi Arabia are incompatible with the abuse of older persons. Older persons who suffer neglect, violence or abuse can call the general hotline (telephone number 1919) at the Domestic Violence Reporting Centre, available free of charge and round the clock for victims of all ages. 66. While the Independent Expert commends the profound respect for older persons, deeply rooted in Saudi Arabia’s religious and cultural traditions, in most countries violence against older persons is a largely underreported crime owing to the shame and social stigmatization associated with it. Cultural norms that emphasize respect for older persons can and should serve as a strong foundation for legal and policy frameworks to prevent abuse. Research shows that the abuse of older persons – whether physical, emotional, verbal or economic, among others – is frequently hidden and underreported and occurs across all societies and income levels. Shame, dependence on the abuser, fear of retaliation and lack of awareness of rights are all factors that suppress reporting. 67. States Parties to the Convention against Torture have the obligation under articles 2 and 16 to prevent cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, including in domestic and care settings. Article 16 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires States to prevent all forms of exploitation, violence and abuse of persons with disabilities, including age-related disabilities, both within and outside the home. The abuse of older persons, when it causes severe pain or suffering, falls within the scope of ill-treatment under both conventions. In this regard, the Independent Expert underlines that violence, abuse and neglect of older persons must be treated as a human rights issue requiring robust legal, institutional and social responses. 68. There are no official data on the extent of domestic violence against women in Saudi Arabia, and many of the studies conducted exclude older women from their research. The Independent Expert notes that the absence of comprehensive data limits the State’s ability to meet its obligations to protect older women from abuse. She also notes that the persistence of a de facto system of male guardianship and the inadequate criminalization of marital rape, highlighted by the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, increase the risks faced by older women. In 2024, Saudi Arabia received and accepted a recommendation made by Portugal that it criminalize all forms of gender-based violence and improve complaint and reporting mechanisms in that context, especially for women migrant workers.

records.text: 62. The Independent Expert visited several social clubs and diwaniyas across the country. They were all well-equipped, and many offered an impressive range of equipment and services, including day care, physiotherapy, swimming pools, adapted physical exercise and social and cultural activities. The Independent Expert positively noted the growing amount on offer in terms of spaces for socialization and activities that promoted the healthy and active ageing of older persons. These initiatives contribute to fulfilling older persons’ rights to participation in cultural life, leisure and social inclusion, as enshrined in article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It also aligns with target 3.4 of the Sustainable Development Goals, on promoting mental health and well‐being, especially through the prevention of isolation and age-related decline. The availability of recreational and therapeutic spaces designed for older persons supports physical and mental health, increases autonomy and helps reduce the risk of institutionalization. Moreover, age-friendly social spaces contribute to combating negative stereotypes about ageing. 63. However, the Independent Expert observed that most centres were catered for higher-income older persons, such as retired civil servants and businesspersons, and all of them targeted Saudi citizens. Some did include women’s sections, and social clubs for older women were planned to be opened in Riyadh, although at a slower rate than male-only social clubs. The Independent Expert was informed that they are open for all, but was not informed about any specific attempt to ensure the inclusion of older persons who are non-citizens or lower-income Saudi nationals. As a result, she did not observe any non-citizens in the facilities she visited, even though they constitute 30.1 per cent of the country’s population aged 60 and above. 64. This lack of inclusion non-citizens and lower-income individuals raises concerns regarding equal access to cultural participation. In relation to women, the Independent Expert visited many well-equipped and -attended initiatives for women, but the gender imbalance in access to social clubs – with a lower number of clubs for women – reflects ongoing disparities in opportunities for older women to benefit from services that support well-being and social engagement. Under article 13 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, States Parties have the obligation to eliminate discrimination against women in recreational, cultural and social activities. The slower expansion of women’s social clubs may constitute discrimination if older women are systematically left without comparable access.

records.text: 58. Saudi Arabia is making considerable efforts towards gender equality. From 2006 to 2024, women’s participation in the labour force nearly doubled, from 22.5 per cent to 43.2 per cent. In 2024, the country gained five positions in the Global Gender Gap Index of the World Economic Forum, from 131st in 2023 to 126thin 2024. It sits sixth in that ranking out of 15 States in the Middle East and Northern Africa, and ranks sixty-seventh worldwide in terms of educational attainment. These improvements reflect the Government’s ongoing efforts under Saudi Vision 2030, including opportunities for women in labour and education. The Kingdom’s ratification in 2000 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women also reflected its commitment to the elimination of discrimination against women in all areas of life. 59. However, older women still face discrimination and cumulative disadvantages in many areas of life. Given historically lower participation in the formal workforce and lower salaries, they face disproportionately lower incomes and pensions, or no pension after retirement. Their role as caregivers of grandchildren, spouses, older parents and relatives, some with disabilities, often means that their own care needs are ignored. This trend reflects a broader pattern of gender discrimination, where older women’s unpaid and informal care work throughout their life cycle limits their access to contributory social protection schemes at later life stages. Older women’s contributions as caregivers need to be formally recognized and supported through non-contributory pension schemes and access to respite services, in line with target 5.4 of the Sustainable Development Goals, and with article 11 (1) (e) of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, on women’s right to social security. 60. The Independent Expert visited some social facilities exclusively for women, with dedicated sections for recreation, sports, well-being and socializing. They were well attended, mostly by older women from advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds. These centres facilitate the rights to cultural and economic participation of older and younger women, as well intergenerational exchanges in a women-only setting. The Independent Expert was positively impressed by the huge range of activities, from traditional crafts to digital skills, offered in an intergenerational female setting. 61. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women has noted that women, including older women, are considered not as full rights holders but primarily as caregivers for children and older relatives, owing to persisting gender stereotypes, despite the Government’s efforts to change sociocultural patterns and patriarchal attitudes. This situation is incompatible with a rights-based approach to ageing, which requires that older women be treated as autonomous rights holders, in line with the principles of non-discrimination and equality for all persons and with the obligations of Saudi Arabia under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Arab Charter on Human Rights (arts. 3 and 33).

records.section: Main findings and challenges E. Deprivation of liberty
records.text: 47. The Independent Expert examined the situation of older persons deprived of liberty in Saudi Arabia. With that purpose, she visited Al-Ha’ir prison in Riyadh, the largest detention facility in the country, with a population of 1,006 inmates. The data provided to the Independent Expert on older persons being held in Al-Ha’ir prison was very scarce: she was informed that 82 of the prisoners were older persons, all of them men and none in the maximum security regime. The importance of maintaining data on detainees that is disaggregated by age and health is reflected in rules 6 and 7 of the Nelson Mandela Rules, and is essential to ensure the well-being of each detainee. 48. The facilities visited by the Independent Expert were clean, well lit and spacious. Each of the cells included in the visit had access to its own small outdoor patio. The medical facilities included a modern and fully-equipped and -staffed hospital, with the capability of conducting magnetic resonance imaging, X-rays and surgical operations, and offering dental, dermatological, ophthalmological and orthopaedic care and physical rehabilitation services, among others. Its staff comprised 50 doctors and 120 nurses, and it offered all services free of charge. These services demonstrate efforts to comply with the Nelson Mandela Rules, particularly rule 24, which affirms the right of prisoners to enjoy the same standards of healthcare that are available in the community. 49. The Independent Expert noted that the existence of an office of the Human Rights Commission inside the facilities was a positive step. However, the official in charge told the Independent Expert that he did not have any information about the number of older detainees or the main issues affecting them, even though the Independent Expert’s visit was not impromptu or unannounced. He also stated that he did not carry out any specific work to protect or promote the rights of older prisoners. This absence of specific oversight with regard to older prisoners risks neglecting their needs and vulnerabilities. Older persons can face heightened vulnerability owing to physical frailty, cognitive decline and chronic illness, which require specific monitoring and response. 50. Al-Ha’ir prison had an impressive variety of educational, cultural, entertainment and sports equipment and activities, including an indoor multi-sports pitch, musical instruments, traditional dancing, recording and broadcasting studios, a café, video games and several publications produced by prisoners. However, none of them was specifically tailored to older persons. The absence of age‐sensitive programming can result in the de facto exclusion of older persons from participation, undermining their rights under rule 105 of the Nelson Mandela Rules. Recreational opportunities should be adapted to reflect the capacities and preferences of older detainees 51. Older persons that the Independent Expert spoke to said that they enjoyed free access to the common facilities for most of the day, while they were required to stay enclosed in their cells at night-time only. They also stated that they were treated respectfully by prison officials. 52. On the day before the visit to Al-Ha’ir prison, the Independent Expert communicated to the Government that she intended to talk to Mr. Al-Hawali (75-year-old man with disabilities) and to a prominent human rights defender, Mr. Salman al-Awdah (68-year-old man), who were being held there. Their incarceration, risk of execution, prison conditions and denial of healthcare had raised concerns in the United Nations human rights system. 53. Regrettably, the prison authorities rejected the Independent Expert’s request, allegedly for lack of time to arrange her access, even though it was made 24 hours in advance. The refusal to allow the visit to Mr. Al-Hawali and Mr. Al-Awdah violated the terms of reference for country visits by special procedure mandate holders, which includes the right to establish confidential and unsupervised contact with persons deprived of their liberty. Blocking access to potentially at-risk detainees can limit the ability to document and prevent violations against them. 54. An aspect observed in the visit that did not meet the Nelson Mandela Rules was that prisoners who were employed in Al-Ha’ir prison did not receive any remuneration (rule 103 (1)). Instead, in exchange for work, they received benefits, such as an increased number of family visits. This practice not only violates their right to equitable remuneration, but also their right to family visits, which should not be used as an incentive, but should be guaranteed as a right that may be restricted only when strictly necessary and in a proportionate manner. 55. Saudi Arabia has acceded to the Convention against Torture, but not to the Optional Protocol thereto, under which a double-tier system of prevention is established based on a national mechanism and regular visits by an international mechanism, the Subcommittee on Prevention of Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. In 2024, the Government accepted a recommendation made by Ghana that it consider ratifying the Optional Protocol. The Independent Expert regrets the very limited data on the number, gender, age, health status and legal basis for the detention of older persons provided during her visit. This absence of transparency impedes effective monitoring and accountability, and raises concerns about the ability of older persons to obtain access to safeguards and remedies. 56. The Independent Expert received information that some older persons, particularly those accused of security-related offences or dissent, remained in prolonged pretrial detention or served extended sentences without access to regular judicial review or adequate healthcare. The Independent Expert is concerned that individuals over the age of 60 may be regularly held in arbitrary detention, without clear legal justification and/or in inhumane conditions, raising questions about compliance with the principles of legality, necessity and proportionality. Where such conditions cause severe physical or mental suffering, especially in the absence of medical care, they may amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under article 16 of the Convention against Torture. Older persons are particularly susceptible to harm from inadequate detention conditions, and prolonged pretrial detention without judicial oversight can further exacerbate their vulnerability. 57. The Independent Expert recalls that deprivation of liberty must always be a measure of last resort, subject to strict safeguards and in full accordance with international standards, including the Nelson Mandela Rules, the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Older persons are entitled to procedural guarantees, age-appropriate accommodation, access to healthcare and regular review of their detention. In additional, they require individualized assessments and reasonable accommodation to ensure that detention conditions do not amount to ill-treatment owing to their age-related vulnerabilities.

records.text: 40. Under the Basic Law of Governance, the State is responsible for public health and provides healthcare for every citizen. In practice, this provision has been implemented through a public healthcare system that offers comprehensive medical care largely free of cost to its citizens. The Independent Expert witnessed the results of the investments made in the health sector and observed the country’s impressive capacity in this regard. This national commitment to healthcare is aligned with article 39 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights, which affirms the right of every person to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health services. 41. The Government also funds and promotes groundbreaking research on healthy ageing. The Independent Expert visited, for example, Hevolution Foundation, a pioneering organization launched in 2021 for research and innovation regarding the biology of ageing, with an annual budget of up to 1 billion dollars. The foundation fosters global scientific discovery, new therapies and start‐ups in the area of ageing. 42. The Independent Expert visited several health centres, including Seha Virtual Hospital, recognized as the world’s largest virtual hospital. It connects 224 health centres and offers 44 specialized services, including cardiology, critical care, neurology and psychiatry, enabling older patients, among others, to receive expert care remotely, either in their own domiciles or in health centres outside the larger urban centres where a particular medical specialty is not available. Many health centres also offer at-home healthcare to patients, including not only visits by nurses and general practitioners, but also specialized care (including dental care), dialysis treatment and the provision and adaptation of assistive devices in the domiciles of older persons. These community‐based and home-based healthcare models are essential for realizing the rights of older persons to live independently and to have access to health services that are responsive to their needs, as set forth in articles 19 and 25 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. They also contribute to reducing institutionalization and enable ageing in place. 43. However, older persons who are not Saudi citizens do not have the right to obtain free healthcare in the public health system. Instead, they are obliged to subscribe to private insurance – paid by themselves or their employers – even though the foreign population of the country is largely composed of lower-income labourers and non-specialized workers in situations of economic vulnerability. This exclusion raises concerns under the principles of non-discrimination and universality in the right to health, contrary to article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which affirms that medical care must be available to all. By conditioning access to free, public healthcare on citizenship, the current policy potentially undermines the right to health for a large proportion of older persons residing in the country. 44. During the response to the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, the Government provided vaccinations universally, including non-citizens and undocumented migrants, showing a commendable example of health policy benefiting from the inclusion of all persons irrespective of their legal status in the country. This inclusive approach shows that Saudi Arabia has the capacity to implement non-discriminatory access to health services, and it should be encouraged to apply similar principles beyond emergency responses. 45. Geriatric medicine was formally recognized as a specialty in Saudi Arabia only recently. The Saudi Commission for Health Specialties introduced the Geriatric Medicine Fellowship training programme in 2021, marking a positive step in the formalization of geriatric medicine within the medical education system. Before the creation of the training programme, training in geriatric medicine in Saudi medical schools was limited, both in undergraduate and postgraduate education. Currently, Saudi Arabia has only 48 geriatricians and 26 medical doctors specialized in family medicine for older persons, for a population exceeding one million persons aged 65 and above. As training in geriatrics is currently being offered in medical schools in the country, it is feasible to promptly scale up the number of trained professionals. 46. During her visit to Al-Ha’ir prison in Riyadh, the Independent Expert observed an impressive range of general and specialized healthcare services offered to prisoners, with advanced equipment and staff, including 50 medical doctors and a magnetic resonance imaging device. However, the Independent Expert notes that the denial of medical care may be being used to target specific prisoners, according to the information received. The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities concluded in 2024 that Safar bin Abdulrahman al-Hawali, a prominent religious scholar being held in Al-Ha’ir prison, had been denied appropriate medical care. States have a heightened obligation to provide medical treatment to persons in detention. The deliberate denial thereof may constitute cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. When it disproportionately affects older prisoners and those with disabilities, it may also amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under article 15 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. It can also violate the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules), particularly rule 24, which stipulates that prisoners should enjoy the same standards of healthcare that are available in the community. Under the Nelson Mandela Rules, access to healthcare must be provided without discrimination, meaning that it cannot be withheld as a coercive measure.

records.text: 36. The Elderly Rights and Care Act emphasizes institutional and family care, but does not enshrine the right to live independently and be included in the community, contrary to article 19 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Independent Expert was informed that Saudi culture strongly favours the provision of care to older persons within the family, and that there is social stigma attached to having older parents live in care homes. Multigenerational living is common and, traditionally, extended families – often several generations – live together under one roof. While this model has long offered familial protection, it relies disproportionately on unpaid care work by women, constituting a structural barrier to the enjoyment of many human rights, including women’s full economic participation, right to education, and access to social security. It is also incompatible with article 11 of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, under which States Parties are required to ensure equal access to social security and to eliminate discrimination against women in the fields of employment and family responsibilities. 37. Urbanization has caused a fast shift towards nuclear-family households, and in 2022, the average Saudi family consisted of 4.8 members. Owing to urbanization and demographic changes, the family support model is increasingly being put under stress. Many interlocutors shared anecdotes with the Independent Expert about how most families were struggling to maintain that model. As women enter the formal workforce and family structures evolve, the need for public support mechanisms for the care of older persons is likely to rise. Such mechanisms include community‐based care services, respite care, financial assistance to family caregivers, and awareness-raising campaigns to enhance the social value of caregiving. These measures are essential to ensure the rights of older persons to an adequate standard of living, to health and to live independently, in line with the principles of autonomy, dignity and equality. Ensuring that caregiving is supported, socially recognized and equitably shared also corresponds with target 5.4 of the Sustainable Development Goals, on recognizing and valuing unpaid care and domestic work through the provision of public services and social protection policies. 38. Domestic care workers, most of them migrant women, play an important role in providing care to Saudi older persons. However, they are excluded from the protection of the Labour Code. The kafalah system of sponsorship that binds their legal status to their employer exposes them to a high risk of economic and physical abuse, trafficking and exploitation. The kafalah system was abolished or limited for most sectors of the workforce in 2021, but remained for domestic workers. Employers do not receive penalties for withholding the passports of domestic workers or for failing to provide adequate housing, food, medical expenses or weekly rest days. There is no effective mechanism for reporting such abuses, and Saudi Arabia has not ratified Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), of the International Labour Organization (ILO). This situation may be incompatible with articles 10 and 34 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights, on the prohibition of forced labour and on fair conditions of work for all. 39. The Independent Expert visited homes for older persons without relatives, some organized as independent, fully-equipped apartments and others as nursing homes. All facilities were in excellent condition. They provided adequate living conditions for their residents and seemed to offer respectful and positive environments. The Independent Expert also positively noted that, contrary to practices in other contexts, residents who were still autonomous could freely leave and return to the facilities unrestricted, in line with their right to liberty of movement and their right to make choices about their lives, as affirmed in articles 14 and 19 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. This good practice in institutional care should be further complemented by developing non‐institutional and community-based options, to ensure that care reflects the needs, autonomy and dignity of older persons. Ideally, locating care homes in central locations, where residents have access within walking distance to local services and resources, would be ideal to promote their autonomy.

records.section: Main findings and challenges B. Right to social security and social protection
records.text: 29. Saudi Arabia has public contributory and non-contributory pension systems. Contributory public retirement pensions are managed by the General Organization for Social Insurance, with 1.8million beneficiaries, including more than 960,000 pensioners and 881,000 “heirs”: heirs include not only spouses and dependent children but also parents, many of whom are older persons, thus contributing to their right to an adequate standard of living. In another positive aspect, the General Organization for Social Insurance has a high replacement ratio: currently averaging at 76 per cent, members contributing for a period of 40 years and retiring after the minimum retirement age (currently 60, increased to 65 for those newly entering the workforce) can receive a rate of 100per cent of their last salary before retirement. The General Organization for Social Insurance has made notable efforts to improve accessibility, offering a wide range of both offline and online services, including a home visit programme for members who require support and face challenges reaching its offices. 30. However, the coverage offered by the General Organization for Social Insurance among the wider population of older persons remains limited, with only 24.5 per cent of persons aged 60 and above receiving a contributory pension from that programme. Non-citizen older persons, comprising 30.1 per cent of the population of that age, are excluded, as are informal workers. Excluding non‐citizens, who comprise 77 per cent of the country’s workforce, is contrary to provisions in international law providing for everyone’s right to social security and to an adequate standard of living without discrimination. Relevant standards include articles 22 and 25 (1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, article 28 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and article 11 (1) (e) of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women. The exclusion also contradicts articles 3 (1), 36 and 38 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights, which affirm the equal right of all individuals to social security and to an adequate standard of living without discrimination. Officials at the General Organization for Social Insurance have assured the Independent Expert that the Government plans to include migrant workers in its contributory pension system, an encouraging step to ensure their right to an adequate standard of living when they reach retirement age. 31. The non-contributory system is integrated under the new social Protection Strategy and the Citizen Account Programme, is regulated by the Social Security Act (Royal Decree No. M/32 (2020)) and is administered by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development. It provides an essential safety net for low-income older persons, especially those without a formal employment history. Its eligibility criteria are based on households, with a threshold of approximately 1,320 riyals (SRl) (approximately US$ 352) per capita. The head of household receives approximately SRl 1,320 per month, with an additional amount of SRl 660 per month for each dependent. 32. However, some factors pose obstacles to the accessibility of non-contributory pensions. First, older persons who are not Saudi citizens (30.1 per cent of the population aged 60 and above) are not eligible, leaving them at the risk of economic vulnerability in contravention of the international standards mentioned in paragraph 20 above. Second, there is a risk of the system’s digital nature leaving older persons with limited literacy or Internet access behind, highlighting the need for age‐sensitive adaptations and the importance of ongoing efforts to deliver digital assistance through field teams that visit older persons at home. 33. Social security benefits must be adequate in amount and duration so that everyone is able to realize their rights to family protection and assistance, to an adequate standard of living and to healthcare. However, the individual benefit cap in Saudi Arabia is SRl 1,320 (approximately US$352) per month, which constitutes one third of the minimum monthly salary for Saudi nationals (SRl 4,000) and 13 per cent of the average monthly salary (SRl 10,016). This amount is not automatically adjusted for inflation or differences in the cost of living, which can negatively affect older persons residing in major cities such as Riyadh or Jeddah, where the cost of living far exceeds that of smaller towns and rural areas. 34. As a result of the obstacles mentioned above and the limited amount in non-contributory pensions, older persons with limited family support, especially women and persons living alone, may fall below the national poverty line despite receiving benefits. While Saudi Arabia does not publish official poverty data, the Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia estimates that the poverty rate is approximately 13.6 per cent among Saudi nationals. and the rate is very likely to be higher among non-nationals. The absence of long-term care benefits under both contributory and non-contributory pensions further burdens older persons, as the need for care is presumed to be met by families, without financial or institutional support. 35. A large part of the social protection work is being carried out by Government-sponsored associations. The Independent Expert commends the generosity of philanthropists and volunteers who work on the assistance of older persons in vulnerability. Their work is monitored by the National Centre for Non-Profit Sector Development, but the Independent Expert did not receive details on the standards used in the monitoring, or about mechanisms for ensuring accountability for the work that they carry out. The Independent Expert observed that the approaches of each organization to social assistance were very different in practice. In absence of a social protection floor for all older persons (irrespective of which non-profit organization is assisting them) and of clear standards on the quality of the assistance provided, and given that the non-citizen population is excluded, this charitable approach lacks a rights-based perspective and is incompatible with the rights of everyone to social security and to an adequate standard of living without discrimination, set forth in articles 22 and 25(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and articles 3 (1), 36 and 38 of the Arab Charter on Human Rights.

records.section: Main findings and challenges A. Accessibility
records.text: 20. Throughout the visit, the Independent Expert observed remarkable efforts to ensure the physical accessibility of public spaces, infrastructure, transportation services and government services for older persons with limited mobility. These efforts reflect the increasing attention paid to ensuring equal access and inclusion in line with article 9 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to which Saudi Arabia Acceded in 2008. Under the Convention, States Parties are required to take appropriate measures to ensure that persons with disabilities – including older persons with age-related disabilities – have access, on an equal basis with others, to the physical environment, to transportation, to information and communications and to other facilities and services open or provided to the public. The Government’s efforts are also in line with target 11.7 of the Sustainable Development Goals, on providing universal access to safe, inclusive and accessible green and public spaces for all. 21. One of the most prominent examples was the Haramain High-Speed Railway, connecting the cities of Mecca and Medina via Jeddah and used by millions of pilgrims every year travelling for the hajj and umrah. Dozens of wheelchairs, including electric wheelchairs, are immediately accessible to any person who requires them, in particular older persons, upon reaching the station in Jeddah, which also has dedicated queues and seating areas for older persons. With older persons making up 30 per cent of its millions of users (7 million in 2023), the railway has shown an outstanding commitment to serving its oldest passengers. 22. Another positive example noted by the Independent Expert was the establishment of multiple parks, green spaces and walking areas across the country, including the recently developed Sports Boulevard in Riyadh, where older persons, among others, can walk and exercise outdoors. Such projects contribute to healthy ageing by supporting older persons’ physical and mental well-being, participation and community life. As physical exercise is not currently common for most older persons in Saudi Arabia, these projects can contribute to a cultural change to make them more physically active. In order to be accessible and attractive in practice to older persons, such projects should be located within walking distance from their residences, as some of them require travel for considerable distances by car or public transportation (where available) from most neighbourhoods. 23. Remarkably, all municipal offices visited by the Independent Expert have dedicated parking spots, priority lines, counters and sitting areas for older persons. Some of them centralize attention on older persons at single counters to avoid them having to walk to different offices to obtain services, thus reducing administrative burdens on older persons and enhancing their autonomy and dignity. 24. The Independent Expert visited King Abdullah Sports City stadium in Jeddah, which offers older persons priority parking and seating access. It also has extensive areas dedicated to persons using wheelchairs. These features show a promising approach to making the 2034 FIFA World Cup accessible to older persons attending the games. The inclusive design of sports infrastructure aligns with the right to participate on an equal basis with others in cultural and sporting life, enshrined in article 30 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 25. Another commendable effort towards accessibility for older persons is the system used by the Civil Affairs Agency of the Ministry of Interior to enhance access to civil affairs services for citizens in remote areas and those with limited mobility. Under initiatives such as the “We Come to You” and “We Exist” schemes, mobile units deliver services including the issue and renewal of national identity cards. For persons aged 85 and above, the “Taqdeer” programme offers services at their homes, hospitals or care facilities. Additionally, the “Absher” platform offers a wide range of virtual civil affairs services. These efforts support the rights of older persons to legal recognition and access to documentation, which can facilitate access to other rights such as the rights to health or social protection. It should be noted, though, that despite efforts to make the system largely accessible, many older persons still require the help of relatives or public officials to use it. Ensuring digital literacy and accessible design is therefore vital. 26. The Government’s investments in digitalization may potentially improve access to services and efficiency in administrative processes. However, some older persons continue to face challenges in using digital platforms independently owing to limited digital literacy, visual or cognitive impairments or lack of access to devices. Without support, such as in-person assistance and an age‐friendly design, there is a risk that digital services may negatively affect older persons. 27. Among the areas where increased efforts towards accessibility are still required, the Independent Expert observed that the new Riyadh Metro, inaugurated in November 2024, was still lacking certain features of accessibility. While public transportation can enhance the mobility of older persons and contribute to their participation in Saudi society and economy, certain aspects of the Metro require improvement, including the limited number of lifts and lack of audio announcements of floor numbers, maps in small fonts that are very difficult to read and the lack of dedicated queues and seats. These shortcomings may limit the realization of the right of older persons to personal mobility and undermine their full inclusion in the urban environment. The Haramain High-Speed Railway could serve as a practical example to ensure the Metro’s accessibility for older persons. In a country still heavily reliant on car-based transportation, making the Metro truly accessible to all older persons could be crucial for their mobility and autonomy. 28. A large-scale housing project that the Independent Expert visited in Riyadh, the Al-Fursan suburb, is still under construction by the National Housing Company and will house around 250,000persons. It will develop meeting and exercise areas and shops within walking distance from each housing unit, which will benefit older persons. However, in the units visited by the Independent Expert, full accessibility was not included by default, but would be offered only at the request of buyers. Modifying housing in the future to make it accessible as their residents age, or if they develop disabilities, will be more costly and inconvenient than making all units accessible at their conception. Concerns are therefore raised under article 9 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, under which States Parties are required to ensure access to housing on an equal basis with others. Ensuring the accessibility of all housing built by the National Housing Company would benefit not only older persons, but persons of all ages, and would be consistent with the principle of universal design, as defined in article 2 of the Convention.

records.text: 11. Saudi Arabia is a State Party to various conventions that contribute to the protection of the rights of older persons, including the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. It has also ratified the Arab Charter on Human Rights, which includes the rights of all persons to health, education and social security. 12. In 2024, the Government accepted the recommendation made during the universal periodic review that it ratify the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. Starting the process of ratification would constitute a key step towards protecting the rights of older migrants in the country. The Convention is one of the few international instruments that include age as a prohibited ground of discrimination. 13. Under article 27 of the Basic Law of Governance, the State guarantees the rights of citizens and their families in cases of emergency, illness, disability and old age, and supports the social insurance system and encourages institutions and individuals to participate in charitable activities. 14. Age is not included among the prohibited grounds of discrimination in the constitutional framework of Saudi Arabia, meaning that it fails to protect older persons from discrimination at the constitutional level. A positive step to ban age-based discrimination was the amendment in 2024 of its Labour Code, article 61 of which prohibits discrimination based on age (among other grounds) in the labour market. 15. The Elderly Rights and Care Act (2022) codifies essential rights such as the rights to dignity, autonomy and protection from abuse for persons aged 60 and above. However, it does not explicitly prohibit age-based discrimination in employment, healthcare or access to services. Older women are not explicitly mentioned in the text, despite the intersectional discrimination that they suffer. It also lacks references to older persons’ rights to participation in public life, decision-making and consultation on policies affecting them. The Act proclaims the rights to financial support, housing and healthcare, but does not regulate their scope, coverage or adequacy. 16. Within the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, the Elderly Committee forms part of the Family Affairs Council and is chaired by the Minister. The Ministry also runs a care programme for older persons, but the Government lacks an overall comprehensive, rights-based national strategy for older persons, including monitoring and accountability mechanisms. 17. The Human Rights Commission, a government entity directly linked to the King, carries out a broad mandate on the rights of older persons, which encompasses monitoring, investigation of violations and awareness-raising activities on the basis of human rights and Islamic law. 18. The Saudi Vision 2030 programme offers an ambitious framework for modernization and economic and social development, but it lacks a rights-based approach concerning older persons. The rights to equality, non-discrimination and participation are not explicitly mentioned, and the programme does not entail a commitment to universal social protection floors for older persons, which risks leaving older women, migrants, informal workers and other groups behind in the country’s social development efforts. 19. The Government’s commitment to the international promotion and protection of the human rights of older persons was demonstrated by its co-sponsoring, as part of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf, of Human Rights Council resolution 58/13. In that resolution, the Human Rights Council created an open-ended intergovernmental working group with the mandate of elaborating and submitting to it a draft international legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons with the objective of promoting, protecting and ensuring the full enjoyment of human rights by older persons.

records.text: 5. According to the 2022 census, the population of Saudi Arabia has reached 32.2 million, 58.4 per cent of whom Saudi nationals and 41.6 per cent non-Saudi nationals. The median age remains young, at 29.6 years in 2025. However, the country is undergoing demographic changes that will have deep and lasting implications for the realization of the rights of older persons and for social and economic policy. Generally, the Government is aware of the challenges posed by the demographic shift and is committed to adapting its policies to the upcoming changes. 6. According to the United Nations Population Fund, the number of persons aged 60 and above is expected to increase fivefold between 2020 and 2050, from 2 million (5.9 per cent of the total population) to 10.5 million (23.7 per cent). In the same period, the number of persons aged 15 to 24 is expected to increase by only a tenth. Fertility rates have quickly reduced, from 7.7 births per woman in 1967 to 2.3 in 2023. 7. Life expectancy at birth has significantly increased, from 67.32 years for men and 70.68 for women in 1990 to 77.56 years for men and 81.51 years for women in 2025. Women live longer than men, but are more likely to experience economic vulnerability in old age owing to lower labour-force participation (particularly due to their role as primary caregivers) and limited access to contributory pension schemes. This situation highlights the need for gender-sensitive policies with regard to ageing, consistent with the principles of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, and particularly with general recommendation No. 27 (2010), on older women and the protection of their human rights, of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, in which the Committee focuses on the cumulative disadvantages faced by older women. 8. Saudi Arabia is undergoing a very fast urbanization of its population. In 1960, only 31 per cent of residents lived in urban areas, while that figure reached 85 per cent in 2023 and is estimated to keep growing. This rapid urbanization puts stress on social services and traditional family support systems for older persons, often leading to isolation. 9. Saudi Arabia has the seventh highest percentage of migrants in the world (excluding smaller States with a population of under one million), with non-Saudi nationals making up 41.6 per cent of its population, according to the 2022 census. Foreigners make up approximately 77 per cent of the country’s workforce. Non-Saudi nationals also represent a substantial part of the population in older age groups: 39.7 per cent of those aged 60 to 64, 30.2 per cent of those aged 65 to 69, 24.2 per cent of those aged 70 to 74, 15.9 per cent of those aged 75 to 79 and 12.7 per cent of those aged 80 and above are non-citizens. 10. In 2024, the old-age dependency ratio was 4 per cent, with 25.85 million people aged 15 to 64 (73 per cent of the total population), compared to 1.04 million aged 65 and above (3 per cent), according to World Bank estimates. As the population ages, the old-age dependency ratio is expected to rise significantly, showing the urgency of adapting legal frameworks, social protection systems, healthcare services and community support structures to meet the needs and rights of a diverse and ageing population with a large proportion of non-citizens.

records.text: 48. Recalling its general recommendation No. 30 (2004) on discrimination against non ‐citizens, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Develop and adopt a legal framework in accordance with international standards, particularly the Convention, that provides adequate protection of migrants, asylum-seekers and refugees and establishes an asylum procedure, in accordance with internationally recognized standards, including the principle of non-refoulement; (b) En sure that immigration detention is applied only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest possible period, after an assessment of its legality, necessity and proportionality on a case-by-case basis; (c) Take measures to improve the living conditions in detention facilities for migrants and asylum-seekers in accordance with international standards and ensure that everyone in those facilities has access to medical care, interpreters, adequate food and social support; (d) Conduct effective, thorough and impartial investigations into all reports of abuses and violations of human rights perpetrated against migrants and asylum ‐ seekers, particularly those committed in detention facilities and at the State party’s border with Yemen, prosecute and punish adequately those convicted with penalties commensurate with the offences, and provide victims of discriminatory acts with adequate redress and support; (e) Refrain from collective expulsion, deportation and pushback, provide access to its territory for persons in need of international protection, respect the principle of non ‐ refoulement, and conduct investigations into cases of collective expulsion, pushback and excessive use of force and violence by law enforcement officials against migrants, refugees and asylum-seekers; (f) Review its legal framework on the lethal use of force by border law enforcement officials to ensure that it is in accordance with international law and international standards, including the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials, the United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement and the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials.

records.text: 39. The Committee welcomes the measures taken by the State party to implement Cabinet Decree No. 166 of 9 October 2000 to improve the situation of migrant workers, including the launch, in 2020, of the Contractual Relationship Improvement Initiative and the Labour Reform Initiative by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, to facilitate job transfers of migrant workers and their leaving the State party without the permission of the employer, which came into force in March 2021. Nevertheless, the Committee is concerned that: (a) The legal framework on labour still does not provide sufficient protection for migrant workers, in relation to their ability to change jobs and leave the State party, in particular as regards: the requirement to work at least one year with an employer before being able to move to a new employer, the requirement/condition of submitting a complaint against the employer for an abuse such as non-payment of salary or non-renewal of work permit, and the requirement for migrant workers to submit a request to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development in order to leave the State party under a complex administrative procedure and after the payment of a fee; (b) Migrant workers, particularly domestic workers, face discrimination and exclusion under the legislative framework. The prohibition of discrimination in employment under article 3 of the Labour Code only applies to Saudi citizens and excludes migrant workers, the minimum wage applies only to Saudi nationals and there is no minimum wage for migrant workers, and the age of retirement, under article 38 of the Social Insurance Law, does not apply to migrant workers; (c) Lower-income migrant workers, particularly domestic workers, face obstacles and indirect discrimination with regard to family reunification, due to the high wage requirement for sponsoring a family in the State party in relation to the wages they receive and also taking into account the lack of a minimum wage for migrant workers and domestic workers in the legislative framework; (d) Migrant workers, including domestic workers, face discrimination in the exercise of their rights to freedom of association and to form and join trade unions, particularly under the provisions of the Civil Society Associations and Organizations Law and the Labour Code, which exclude migrants from the possibility of establishing civil society organizations and trade unions and joining the latter; (e) Measures taken to protect the occupational health and safety of migrant workers are reportedly ineffective, with reports of a high mortality rate among migrant workers due to harsh working environments, extreme heat and poor living conditions, notwithstanding the information provided by the delegation on the campaigns organized by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development to verify that occupational safety and health checks are carried out as regards working under the sun; (f) Migrant workers are subjected to mandatory HIV/AIDS testing and, if found to be living with HIV, face deportation (arts. 1, 2 and 5).

records.text: 29. The Committee notes the information provided by the delegation that the legislative framework guarantees the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion for members of the Shia ethno-religious minority group and of religions other than Islam. However, the Committee is concerned about reports that ethno-religious minority groups, in particular non‐Sunni ethno-religious minority groups, face obstacles in obtaining permission to construct religious places of worship. It is further concerned about reports that non-citizens, such as migrant workers and domestic workers from Africa and South-East Asia who are non-Muslims, face discrimination in the enjoyment of their right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, which includes restrictions on constructing religious places of worship, on organizing cultural activities with a religious character, such as public worship, and on public displaying of religious symbols (art. 5).

records.section: Criminal justice system and the death penalty
records.text: 26. Recalling its general recommendation No. 31 (2005) on the prevention of racial discrimination in the administration and functioning of the criminal justice system, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Establish a moratorium on the death penalty with a view to abolishing it; (b) Expedite the reform of the justice system and review its legislative framework to ensure that penalties are never imposed for vaguely worded crimes; (c) Ensure the right to fair trial proceedings, while ensuring the availability of legal assistance and the inadmissibility of evidence obtained under duress and torture before court, and prompt, independent and effective investigations of torture and ill ‐ treatment allegations; (d) Adopt measures to ensure gender-responsive application of the law so that evidence of trauma, economic pressure and child marriage, as well as domestic and gender-based violence, are adequately taken into consideration in criminal procedures against women migrant workers and women domestic workers sentenced to death, in line with the relevant recommendations of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women; (e) Collect and publish disaggregated statistics on death sentences imposed and executions carried out, including the type of offence and the demographic data on convicted persons.

records.text: 25. The Committee takes note of the information provided by the State party on the measures to reform the justice system, including the codification of crimes and penalties, and on the protection safeguards in the criminal justice system, such as the mandatory appeal of death penalty sentences and review by the Supreme Court. Nevertheless, the Committee is concerned about reports that: (a) Members of the Shia ethno-religious minority group, migrant workers and domestic workers, including women, are overrepresented in the criminal justice system and disproportionately subjected to arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment along with an absence of fair trial guarantees, and with coerced confessions, particularly in cases involving the death penalty; (b) There has been a significant increase in the rate of executions carried out since 2023, in particular among members of the Shia ethno-religious minority group, migrant workers and domestic workers, while the State party does not make available detailed, disaggregated statistics on death sentences imposed and executions carried out, including the type of offence and the demographic data on convicted persons; (c) Women migrant workers and domestic workers, who experience intersecting discrimination based on gender, language, ethnicity, national origin and class, are sentenced to death without consideration of gender-related factors during criminal proceedings against them, including the domestic and gender-based violence they endured prior to the crime (arts. 2, 5 and 6).

Recalling its general recommendations No. 7 (1985) relating to the implementation of article 4 of the Convention, No. 15 (1993) on article 4 of the Convention and No. 35 (2013) on combating racist hate speech, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Expedite the codification and adoption of the Penal Code and ensure that it explicitly criminalizes racist hate speech and hate crimes in accordance with article 4 of the Convention and includes all the grounds of discrimination recognized in article 1 of the Convention; (b) Review its legal framework, particularly article 8 of the Civil Association and Organization Law, article 9 of the Printing and Publication Law and article 5 of the Audiovisual Media Law, with a view to bringing them into line with the Convention; (c) Enhance its efforts to combat the spread of racist hate speech in the media, on the Internet and in social media, in close cooperation with media outlets, Internet service providers and social media platforms; (d) Firmly condemn any form of hate speech and distance itself from racist hate speech expressed by public figures, including religious leaders, and ensure that such acts are investigated and adequately punished; (e) Improve the system for collecting and disaggregating data on the number and types of complaints of racist hate speech and hate crimes, the number of investigations, prosecutions and convictions, and the reparation provided to victims, disaggregated by age, gender, and ethnic and national origin of the victims and the perpetrators, and include relevant statistics in its next periodic report.

records.text: 19. The Committee notes the information provided by the delegation on the legislative framework to combat hate speech and hate crimes, particularly under article 39 of the Basic Law of Governance, article 8 of the Civil Association and Organization Law, article 9 of the Printing and Publication Law and article 5 of the Audiovisual Media Law. It also takes note that racist motive is considered an aggravating circumstance. The Committee further notes the information provided by the delegation on the revision of school textbooks to remove prejudice and promote understanding. It takes note of the statistics provided by the delegation on cases related to the Audiovisual Media Law and the Printing and Publication Law. The Committee further takes note of information on the codifying and drafting of a Penal Code. Nevertheless, the Committee is concerned: (a) That the legislative framework does not contain provisions that expressly criminalize racist hate speech and hate crimes in accordance with article 4 of the Convention and on all the grounds recognized in article 1; (b) That the criminalization of hate speech and hate crime under the legislative framework is based on vague concepts, such as “undermining public order” or “contradicts public morals”, and that the criminalization of hate speech and hate crimes only applies when nationals are the victims of it, excluding groups vulnerable to racial discrimination such as migrants and stateless persons; (c) About reports of the spread of racist hate speech and the dissemination of negative stereotypes against ethno-religious minority groups, people of African descent, migrants and stateless persons, including on the Internet and social media; (d) About reports of the use of racist hate speech by public figures, including religious leaders, targeting the Shia ethno-religious minority group, and about the lack of information on investigations, prosecutions and convictions of such public figures; (e) About the lack of detailed information on complaints or cases involving hate crimes and hate speech in the State party, prosecutions, and convictions and sanctions imposed on perpetrators, notwithstanding the statistics provided by the delegation on cases related to the Audiovisual Media Law and the Printing and Publication Law (arts. 4 and 6).

Reiterating its previous recommendations, the Committee urges the State party to develop and adopt comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation that contains a clear definition of racial discrimination and encompasses structural, direct, indirect and intersecting forms of discrimination in both the public and private spheres, in accordance with article 1 of the Convention. It also recommends that the State party review its legal framework with a view to bringing it into line with the Convention, explicitly incorporating the principle of equality and the prohibition of racial discrimination on all prohibited grounds, in line with article 1 of the Convention.

records.text: 15. The Committee takes note of the information that justice and equality are guaranteed under article 8 of the Basic Law of Governance and that the domestic legal framework prohibits discrimination. It also takes note that the State party took measures to adopt legislation to prohibit racial discrimination in accordance with the recommendations made by the Saudi Human Rights Commission, contained in its annual report on the human rights situation in 2019, and to develop and adopt legislation to prohibit racial discrimination in accordance with the State party’s obligation under the Convention. Nevertheless, the Committee remains concerned about the lack of comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation containing an explicit definition of racial discrimination on all the grounds enumerated in article 1 of the Convention and expressly prohibiting structural, direct, indirect and intersecting forms of discrimination in the public and private spheres. Furthermore, the Committee is concerned that the domestic legal framework is based on neutral and vague concepts as regards the grounds for prohibiting discrimination, such as “residents”. It is also concerned about the lack of information on the implementation of the prohibition of discrimination in the domestic legal framework, including intersecting forms of discrimination (arts. 1, 2 and 5).

Reiterating its previous recommendations and considering the information from the State party that reviewing the reservations remains under consideration, the Committee recommends that the State party withdraw its broad reservations to the Convention to ensure the full implementation of the Convention in the State party and avoid misinterpretations on equality among States parties in the application of article 22.

records.text: 63. The Committee requests the State party to submit its combined second, third, fourth and fifth periodic reports by 24 July 2026 and to include in them information on the implementation of the recommendations made in the present concluding observations. The Committee also requests the State party to consider submitting the above-mentioned reports under the Committee’s simplified reporting procedure, according to which the Committee prepares a list of issues at least one year prior to the due date set for the report of a State party. The replies of a State party to such a list of issues constitute its report.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 62. The Committee requests the State party to disseminate the present concluding observations widely, including to non-governmental organizations and organizations of persons with disabilities, and to persons with disabilities themselves and members of their families, in national and minority languages, including sign language, and in accessible formats and to make them available on the government website on human rights.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies
Human rights education, trainings & awareness raising
Ratification of & accession to international instruments
affected_persons: Minorities/ racial, ethnic, linguistic, religious or descent-based groups

records.text: 61. The Committee strongly encourages the State party to involve civil society organizations, in particular organizations of persons with disabilities, in the preparation of its periodic report.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 60. The Committee requests the State party to implement the recommendations contained in the present concluding observations. It recommends that the State party transmit the concluding observations for consideration and action to members of the Government and parliament, officials in relevant ministries, local authorities and members of relevant professional groups, such as education, medical and legal professionals, as well as to the media, using modern social communication strategies.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies
Human rights education, trainings & awareness raising

records.text: 59. The Committee emphasizes the importance of all the recommendations contained in the present concluding recommendations. With regard to urgent measures that must be taken, the Committee would like to draw the State party’s attention to the recommendations contained in paragraphs 6, on the national implementation of the Convention, and 28, on freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
